analysis.one_liner: Strengthens online privacy rules for children and teenagers, requiring parental-style consent, banning targeted ads to minors, and letting families sue violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after introduction it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee, where it sat until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the 1998 children's online privacy law to cover teenagers under 18. Services aimed at children would need specific, informed consent before collecting a young person's data; families would gain rights to see, correct, and delete that data; targeted ads to minors would be banned on services they are likely to use; and the FTC could enforce the rules with penalties up to $63,795 per violation, alongside a new right for parents to sue. Despite 19 cosponsors, the bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 13 and teenagers under 18, and their parents. Families would gain consent rights over how apps and websites collect and use young people's data, the ability to see, correct, and delete it, and the power to sue companies that violate the rules. Parents of children under 13 specifically gain the private right of action.

how_it_helps.text: Requires services aimed at children to get express, informed consent before collecting a child's or teenager's personal data, and lets teenagers or parents revoke that consent as easily as they gave it.
Bans targeted personalized advertising to children and teenagers based on their data, online behavior, or traits like income level, on services likely to be accessed by minors.
Gives teenagers and parents the right to see, correct, and delete a company's data about them, and stops companies from cutting off service to people who exercise those rights.

Prohibits processing data in ways shown to harm children's physical, emotional, or developmental well-being, and requires services likely to be used by minors to treat children's best interests as a primary design consideration.

Raises the civil penalty per violation to $63,795, lets parents sue in court (including for punitive damages, with no forced arbitration), and creates an FTC Youth Privacy and Marketing Division to enforce the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Tech platforms, social media companies, and the online advertising industry, which would face consent requirements, data-minimization limits, a ban on targeted ads to minors, fines up to $63,795 per violation, and lawsuits from parents. Compliance costs would fall on every digital service likely to be used by children or teenagers, not just giants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech platforms and the adtech industry

drawbacks.text: The bill requires age assurance — a process to estimate or verify each user's age — on services likely to be accessed by minors, which means collecting some age information from all users and could raise new privacy concerns of its own, though the bill requires that data be minimized and destroyed.

Requiring verifiable parental consent for processing teenagers' data, and barring services from denying service over withheld consent, would impose compliance costs and design changes on a wide range of websites and apps, including smaller and nonprofit operators, which could limit some free services or features for young users.

The private right of action, with punitive damages and no pre-dispute arbitration clauses, would expose platforms to litigation that defenders of the bill see as enforcement but that opponents would call a burden that reaches beyond truly bad actors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for families — control over children's data, a ban on targeted ads to minors, stronger FTC enforcement, and the ability to sue violators — are substantial and address documented harms from online platforms. The costs are real but modest and mostly borne by adtech companies and large platforms, which would need age checks and redesigned consent flows. Legitimate objections: blanket parental-consent rules for teens could complicate privacy tools some teens rely on, and age-assurance requirements raise their own privacy questions, though the bill directs the FTC to keep age-check data minimal and destroy it. On balance the bill's public benefits clearly outweigh its compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its data subcommittee, and never came back out — no markup, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 24, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Four days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it stayed.
No further action was ever recorded; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Adtech companies and platforms that profit from targeting ads at children and teenagers keep that revenue untouched; no one else gained.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to update the 1998 children's online privacy law.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or reported it out, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Large technology and advertising industry interests
against.what_they_did: Opposed strict children's online privacy rules during this Congress's broader privacy debate, including restrictions on targeted advertising to minors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only recorded support was from Democrats (sponsor plus 19 cosponsors); no Republican cosponsor is listed, but the bill died in committee without any recorded votes, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill bans targeted personalized advertising to children and teenagers based on their data or behavior, cutting off a core revenue mechanism for adtech firms and the platforms that rely on targeted ads. It would be a direct financial hit to this industry.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and consumer internet companies
industries.note: Platforms would face consent requirements, data-minimization and deletion duties, security mandates, FTC audits, penalties up to $63,795 per violation, and parental lawsuits. They lose the ability to monetize minors' data but keep operating; the bill does not entrench their role.
